result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_isomorphic()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if this graph is isomorphic to another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9387-L9495){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_isomorphic( other, node_attr=None, edge_attr=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is isomorphic](/assets/graphs/is-isomorphic.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Each side compares graph g with graph h. Left: g is a five-node cycle and h is the same cycle redrawn as a star, so is_isomorphic(h) returns True. Right: h is a triangle with a two-edge tail; it has the same node and edge counts, but its degree-3 node C and degree-1 node E (shown in the accent color) have no match in the cycle, so is_isomorphic(h) returns False." width="100%"} Two graphs are isomorphic if their nodes can be put in one-to-one correspondence so that two nodes are joined in one graph exactly when their partners are joined in the other. In other words, they have the same structure, whatever the labels or the drawing. This method decides it exactly, by searching for such a correspondence (use `find_isomorphism()` to get it). Isomorphism tests are used to: - recognize when two networks (molecules, circuits, workflows) are the same structure - deduplicate a collection of graphs, or check that a transformation preserved structure - compare graphs that also carry categorical data, with `node_attr=` and `edge_attr=` Edge direction must agree (both graphs directed or both undirected), and parallel edges and self-loops must correspond one for one. Labels, IDs and weights are ignored unless named with `node_attr=` or `edge_attr=`, and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Graph` to compare with. It is not modified. [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node attribute name, or list of names, whose values must be equal for matched nodes (a missing attribute counts as `None`). [edge_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional edge attribute name, or list of names, whose values must be equal for matched edges. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graphs are isomorphic (respecting the attributes, if given). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Two graphs $G_1, G_2$ are isomorphic when a bijection $\pi: V_1 \to V_2$ satisfies $(u, v) \in E_1 \iff (\pi(u), \pi(v)) \in E_2$. The search first compares node and edge counts, then runs color refinement (the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm) on both graphs together, starting from the attribute colors: if the refined color classes differ in size, no isomorphism exists, and otherwise only nodes of equal refined color are ever paired. The backtracking search then follows the VF2++ design (Jüttner and Madarasi, 2018): nodes are matched in breadth-first order from a rare, high-degree root, candidates come from the neighbors of already matched nodes, and a look-ahead compares, color by color, how the unmatched neighbors of the two nodes split between the search frontier and the rest of the graph. The worst case is exponential (graph isomorphism has no known polynomial algorithm), but typical graphs, including large random, regular and grid graphs, are decided in milliseconds. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path drawn with different labels is still the same path: ::: {#b0fdb982 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]).add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) g2 = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]).add_edges([("Y", "X"), ("Z", "Y")]) g1.is_isomorphic(g2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: A six-node cycle and two separate triangles have the same degrees (six nodes, six edges, every degree 2), but they are not isomorphic, since one is connected and the other is not: ::: {#e111e1dd .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} hexagon = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6) two_triangles = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(3).add_cycle_graph(3) hexagon.could_be_isomorphic(two_triangles, properties="d"), hexagon.is_isomorphic( two_triangles ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: With `node_attr=`, matched nodes must also agree on an attribute. Both molecules below are a chain of three atoms, but the central atom differs: ::: {#7f7b4920 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} water = ec.Graph().add_nodes([("H1", {"el": "H"}), ("O", {"el": "O"}), ("H2", {"el": "H"})]) water.add_edges([("H1", "O"), ("O", "H2")]) other = ec.Graph().add_nodes([("O1", {"el": "O"}), ("H", {"el": "H"}), ("O2", {"el": "O"})]) other.add_edges([("O1", "H"), ("H", "O2")]) water.is_isomorphic(other), water.is_isomorphic(other, node_attr="el") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
